item.title: What My Therapist Knew Never Reached My Med Check
item.description:
Psychiatry

What My Therapist Knew Never Reached My Med Check

Personal Perspective: My care was split into meds and therapy.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • The 15-minute med check often treats only the measurable and ignores the person being measured.
  • Ritual safety questions poorly predict real risk, yet they still organize the encounter.
  • Biological psychiatry favors the measurable over the slower work of actually knowing a patient.
Source: Cottonbro Studio/Pexels

A key question this column seeks to ask is what psychiatry lost when we traded the talking cure for the prescription pad. I learned the answer as a patient. After a manic psychotic episode, I was committed to a state forensic psychiatric hospital, where my treatment narrowed to a single monthly encounter: a quarter-hour with a psychiatrist I came to call the Robot. The trouble was not only that the visit was brief. It was that it never went beneath the surface of me.

The meeting ran on a fixed circuit. A general question about my mood. Two safety questions, asked in the same flat cadence every time: thoughts of harming yourself, thoughts of harming others. Then the readings: my lithium level, my sleep, the tremor in my hands. The safety questions were the strangest part. A large meta-analysis found that most people who die by suicide had denied such thoughts when a clinician last asked; direct questioning predicts danger poorly. The Robot asked anyway, the way a technician reads a gauge, and did not seem to want the answer. It was a box to check, never a conversation.

Nothing I offered could turn the visit anywhere the instruments could not follow. I had spent months reading about bipolar disorder—memoirs, a thick textbook on manic-depressive illness—trying to grasp how my own mind had come apart. When I brought what I had learned, it slid off him. Months later I found his note from that meeting: he had "provided psychoeducation about bipolar disorder." In the record, the exchange ran one way, from expert to pupil. My understanding of my own illness was not a finding his method could record.

The prescribing fed on itself. When one drug produced a side effect, the answer was usually another drug. I watched long-term patients carry the freight of that logic: 10 or 15 medications at once, tremors, a restless shuffle, the weight gain and metabolic wear of years. It could adjust itself endlessly but never look up from its own numbers.

The Man Who Managed My Brain

Once I asked the Robot about the link between my bipolar disorder and the neurosyphilis I had years earlier, an infection that had reached my brain. He cut me off. "Regardless of how it appeared," he said, "what you have is brain damage. That's what matters." Much of the visit he spent typing; the screen took what attention was left. He was not entirely wrong. But in that one sentence a decade of memory, choice, shame, and effort was pressed flat into a fact about tissue.

The word psychiatry comes from the Greek for healing of the soul. Martin Buber distinguished two ways of standing before another person: the I-Thou, in which you meet him as a whole presence, and the I-It, in which you handle him as an object to be measured and filed. The Robot was fluent in the second, and the whole field has drifted his way. It is far easier to read a blood level and check a box than to sit in what the anthropologist T.M. Luhrmann called the "awkward intimacy" of human encounter. Biological psychiatry won its long war against the talking cure in part because measuring a person is quick and knowing one is not. But the soul answers only to the harder thing.

A profile in The New York Times once caught the shape of the loss: a psychiatrist who had traded 45-minute therapy hours for 15-minute medication visits, because that was what insurance would pay. "I'm very important to them," he said, "but I barely know them." The system had priced knowing them out of the job. None of this is against medicine. I take lithium to this day, and it did what years of the wrong treatment never had. It is against a psychiatry that keeps only the half of itself that can be measured.

Source: Felicity Tai/Pexels

What the Med Check Left Out

Here is the part that took me longest to see. I was not only getting the med check. Every week, in a different office, I met with a psychologist who practiced the older kind of psychiatry, the kind that explores rather than measures. She asked about my childhood, my shame, what had actually happened to me and who I had been before any of it. With her, I was not a set of levels. I was a person with an interior worth entering.

I assume they spoke; the treatment team met. But whatever she came to understand about me never surfaced when the Robot sat down for his monthly check. His 15 minutes proceeded as though her work did not exist, as though the only facts that mattered were the ones a blood draw could produce. He managed my chemistry; she tended the life that chemistry ran through; and nothing she learned was ever allowed to change what he did. She could have corrected the picture in a sentence. Her account of me was not part of the equation.

This is the quiet scandal of the 15-minute med check. Its problem is not only that it is brief. It is that nothing but the measurable is allowed to count: not my reading, not my history, not even the clinician down the hall who knew me best. A field named for the healing of the soul had filed the soul in another office and misplaced the key.

What finally returned me to health was slower and unbillable: the return of connection, purpose, and love, the things the Robot never asked about and no dose can supply. Those things mend a mind; none can be prescribed.

And psychiatry is preparing to move further in the wrong direction. Having swapped the awkward intimacy of human encounter for the efficiency of the measurable, the field now stands ready to hand even the 15 minutes to a chatbot that can adjust a dose and check a box without a person present at all. It will be faster and cheaper. And it will complete the retreat the Robot embodied—a psychiatry that can manage a mind to the last decimal and never has to endure the awkward intimacy of knowing whom it treats.

item.title: How Drug Abuse by Bicyclists Led to a Medicine for Psychosis
item.description:
Psychosis

How Drug Abuse by Bicyclists Led to a Medicine for Psychosis

The many pathways to psychotropic drugs.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Similarities between amphetamine toxicity and schizophrenia led Paul Janssen to study amphetamine blockers.
  • In the late 1950s, one such compound, haloperidol, became a major treatment for schizophrenia.
  • In the 1960s, biochemical theories of depression led to the design of molecules resulting in fluoxetine.
  • There are, then, many different pathways to new drugs, including intuition and theory-guided molecule design.

There have been many different pathways to developing psychotropic drugs. None, perhaps, have differed as much as the discovery of haloperidol, which exemplifies the role of creative intuition, and the development of fluoxetine, which came from systematic development of a molecule based on a theory of chemistry underlying mental illness. Let's look at each of these, and see what they say about the genesis of new medicines.

Haloperidol, Haldol

The story of haloperidol began with an observation about the use of performance-enhancing drugs by professional cyclists. Amphetamines were often taken by cyclists in the postwar years, and around 1955, the Belgian physician and pharmacologist Paul Janssen (1926-2003) was told by his colleague Fries Claes that the toxic symptoms they often displayed—including auditory hallucinations, delusions of persecution, thought disorders and stereotyped behaviors—resembled the clinical picture of paranoid schizophrenia. It was not an entirely new observation, having appeared as early as 1938. Indeed, in the early 1950s, several patients appeared in emergency departments of London hospitals with such symptoms, which cleared after admission, and were recognized as coming from what the medical student P.H. Connell named ‘amphetamine psychosis’ in 1953.

Racing cyclists, 2019.
Source: Chabe01 in Wikimedia Commons/Public domain

While Connell’s interest had been in alerting clinicians, Janssen gave these observations a new twist. He had recently founded a research laboratory in Turnhout, Belgium, and was looking for new products. It occurred to him that if amphetamine toxicity turned out to be physiologically similar to schizophrenia, then perhaps a drug which blocked amphetamine’s actions might be a useful treatment for schizophrenia. He was not guided by a theory of a specific chemical underpinning, but recognized that various animal models could represent amphetamine effects. Armed with this approach, he set out to find a substance that might block amphetamine’s actions, which included agitation and stereotyped behavior. He had been working with opioids, and as a starting building block on this new project he used pethidine, which had a structure that could be modified into various analogs relatively easily. He produced and tested a vast number of related compounds. In 1958 he expanded and moved his laboratories to the nearby village of Beerse, where Bert Hermans, one of his chemists, created a butyrophenone, a fluorinated derivative known as R1625, which blocked amphetamine actions in animals and produced behavioral effects—sedation and catalepsy—similar to those of the antipsychotic chlorpromazine. It was tested at Liege Hospital and subsequently at Paris’s St. Anne Hospital, which had played an important role in the development of chlorpromazine; by 1959 haloperidol was marketed in Europe under the brand name Haldol, and later entered the U.S. market in 1967.

Fluoxetine, Prozac

In the 1950s, Janssen’s work leading to haloperidol had no guiding biochemical theory that could explain the actions of haloperidol. By the mid-1960s, the Swedish pharmacologists Arvid Carlsson and Margit Lindqvist, and the Dutch Jacques Van Rossum had recognized dopamine as a neurotransmitter, and they and others presented the hypothesis that its actions were excessive in schizophrenia, but were blocked by drugs such as haloperidol. Similarly, a parallel theory, known as the monoamine hypothesis of depression, began to be presented systematically by the Americans Joseph J. Schildkraut, William E. Bunney and others, suggesting that depression was associated with a decrease in monoamine neurotransmitters such as serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine. This led to an active search for antidepressants which might be more efficacious and with better side effect profiles than the currently available tricyclics and monoamine oxidase inhibitors. This investigation, however, was very different from Janssen’s, as it was guided by a biochemical theory, and brings us to the story of Ray W. Fuller.

Ray W. Fuller (1935-1996) was an Illinois-born biochemist who joined Eli Lilly Company in the early 1960s. He had worked his way through college as an assistant at a large mental hospital; perhaps his experience there led to his lifelong interests in developing medicines for mental illness. Given the understanding of the monoamine hypothesis, in his search for new antidepressants, he developed a system for predicting which drugs might be promising. This was done by giving chloroamphetamine, which lowered brain serotonin, and then testing new compounds to see if they might bring the levels back toward normal. He persuaded Brian B. Malloy (1939-2004), a Scottish-born organic chemist, to join the search. As a starting point, Malloy chose the antihistamine diphenhydramine; it and similar compounds had led to chlorpromazine and imipramine. He began making a series of variations on diphenhydramine and related molecules. In 1971, the team examined the effects of compounds on serotonin in a fraction of homogenized brain tissue known as synaptosomes. The goal was to find something, like imipramine, that would block the reuptake of serotonin and increase the amounts available for neuronal signaling, but unlike imipramine would have less effect on other neurotransmitters. In 1972, they found that fluoxetine was the most powerful agent that met these qualities and pursued it as a drug for humans. In January 1988, Lilly marketed fluoxetine as the antidepressant Prozac, and it was an immediate success. By December, 2.5 million prescriptions had been written, and by 1993, it had been prescribed to 4.5 million Americans. As the years went by, its popularity decreased in favor of newer compounds discovered by similar methods, but it had marked a milestone in the development of psychotropic drugs.

Over time, the fluoxetine process led to many new medicines, including antidepressants that block both serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake (for example, venlafaxine) or dopamine reuptake (bupropion), or binding to specific subtypes of serotonin or norepinephrine receptors (mirtazapine). What they all have in common: They resulted from purposely altering molecules in the context of a biochemical or physiological theory of illness, a process known as rational drug design. This is very different from the method by which many drugs for schizophrenia, bipolar illness, depression, and anxiety were first developed in the 1950s and early 1960s (1), and it produces more predictable results. But it’s good to remember that it came about on the shoulders of an age of new drugs coming from astute discoverers who explored the implications of unexpected observations—like the behavior of intoxicated bicycle racers.

item.title: Mental Health Challenges: Meditate or Medicate?
item.description:
Meditation

Mental Health Challenges: Meditate or Medicate?

The question is not meditate or medicate, but what support is needed to heal.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Healing is rarely an either/or decision.
  • Sometimes the nervous system needs support before the mind can settle.
  • True healing often requires the wisdom to use the right combination of tools.
Source: Africa Studio / AdobeStock

"Trying to 'do' meditation or forcibly manipulating the mind without a proper foundation can lead to mental imbalance, instability, or psychological distress.” — Sadhguru

As a psychotherapist, as well as a student and teacher of mindfulness practices, the question about whether to use meditation or medication to assist with mental health challenges has been on my mind a lot lately. Having recently fallen back into a heightened state of anxiety where both body and mind are noisily making themselves a nuisance, I find myself once again searching for relief. From my decades of practice in behavioral health, I know I share this search with countless others who are often confused, frustrated, and fatigued by the conflicting information available.

Both anxiety and depression are cruel intruders into one’s life. They hijack the brain, sending signals that all is not well with alarming regularity. Hopeless and helpless thoughts are the hallmarks of depression, while fear and panic are the ever-present vibe of anxiety. As a result of the mind-body connection, the feedback loop of irrational thoughts leading to disturbing bodily sensations, leading to negative emotional states, is hard to remove oneself from. This not-so-merry-go-round drives many people to the desperate search for relief.

The meditation or mindfulness movement has found a permanent home in our Western culture, leading to countless books, videos, workshops, retreats, etc that seek to teach this ancient technique to what has historically been a mind-obsessed society. As both a mental health professional and fellow sufferer of anxiety, I jumped on the bandwagon decades ago. The healing power I found carried me through very challenging times, including a cancer diagnosis and its treatment. It was standard procedure for me to meditate while waiting in the oncologist’s office, while sitting in the chemo chair, and while lying on the table waiting for radiation treatment. However, these practices were accompanied and enhanced by modern Western medicine.

Throughout the years, I would discuss with my psychotherapy clients whether or not they have ever considered medication as a means of gaining relief. The responses usually fell into one of two categories, with one being, “I don’t want anything messing with my brain,” and the other being, “Yes please!”

As the meditation movement became more mainstream and moved slightly away from the land of all things woo-woo, I would, when appropriate, discuss whether the client had ever tried or was interested in meditation. I would share that I was using the practice myself and have trained others in the art of watching one’s mind without judgment. To lean in on the sales pitch, I would add that I even taught meditation to rocket scientists at the NASA Langley Research Center.

I continue to receive requests to teach meditation to a variety of individuals across the spectrum. Some have heard of its benefits and want the experience, while others are skeptical but frustrated with other methods of self-regulation and wish to give it a try.

This brings me back to my current state of anxiety and attempts to calm an overly active mind and restless body. Revisiting the successes of the past, I turned to yogic breath techniques, mindful walking, and trying to observe bodily sensations without judgment. While helpful, the anxiety engine continued to rev up, and I realized that if I was going to succeed in bringing forth a more relaxed meditative state, I was going to need help in getting some control over my dysregulated nervous system—it’s nearly impossible to experience a quiet mind when the body feels like it wants to run a marathon.

It has been my standard response when asked how I made it through open heart surgery, 30 rounds of radiation, and four weeks of chemotherapy that it was in a large part due to the medication I was being prescribed to counter the effects of chemo and the steroid drugs to keep me from becoming a wild man. Make no mistake, I was meditating my butt off, and the car that I drove to these daily appointments looked like a New Age shop—replete with aroma therapy oils, worry stones, and printed mantras in easy view.

While scrolling recently through the plethora of YouTube videos that promise relief and release from mental anguish, I found both comfort and confusion. While some of the presenters shared that they had personal experiences with all manner of mental health problems, they clearly had passed through the experience and stood on the other side of the canyon of despair with the assurance that “This helped me get across, and it will help you.” I found some measure of relief watching these videos, both from their mind-distracting nature as well as the flicker of hope that, yes, this will work.

All of this has made me think about how many people suffering from mental distress may turn to the promise of meditation, and its now scientifically proven benefits, and avoid speaking with a qualified medical practitioner to review which medications could assist their recovery. Past clients have often told me that they don’t want to use medication as a crutch. My response is “sometimes using a crutch can prevent further injury.” While medication is not for everyone, neither is meditation. The key element is self-awareness and having a trusted guide. The goal is not to prove our strength through unnecessary suffering. The goal is to heal.

item.title: Rethinking Suicide Through a Neurodivergent Lens
item.description:
Autism

Rethinking Suicide Through a Neurodivergent Lens

We need to ask more nuanced questions about neurodivergence to prevent suicide.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic adults face an eight-fold greater risk of suicide, making neurodivergence a critical risk factor.
  • Standard protocols for crisis intervention and substance use disorders often miss adult autism.
  • Highly stimulating clinical settings and standard therapies can inadvertently worsen neurodivergent distress.
  • Autism screening integrated into routine psychiatric and addiction assessments could save lives.
Person alone holding face in hands in a dark setting.
Source: Daniel R (Mindworld!) / Pixabay

The recent heartbreaking news of two brothers lost to suicide in Adelaide, South Australia, is every family’s worst nightmare. As a psychologist who has spent over two decades working with individuals whose lives have been shaped by addiction, trauma, profound psychological distress, and suicidality, tragedies like this force me to reflect on how clinical protocols often miss critical risk factors long before an acute crisis occurs. Despite national initiatives in both Australia and the U.S., suicide rates remain alarmingly high. What are we missing? To improve outcomes, we must ask more nuanced questions that illuminate the broader context of a crisis, allowing clinicians to identify tailored, effective supports.

The Overlooked Intersection of Autism and Suicidality

One critical, frequently overlooked risk factor in individuals presenting with substance use disorders, self-harm, and suicidal ideation is neurodivergence, particularly autism. This is not speculation regarding the two brothers; none of us can know the exact source of the internal pain described in reports as "overwhelming sensory noise." Rather, their deaths should prompt a broader professional conversation about how to make systems of care more responsive to individual neurodivergent experiences.

In a world built for neurotypical individuals, the pressure to conform is relentless. For an autistic person, navigating social spaces requires immense cognitive effort: interpreting non-verbal cues, forcing eye contact, tolerating sensory overload, and suppressing self-soothing behaviors (stimming).

The empirical evidence linking autism to substance use and suicidality is hard to ignore:

  • A systematic review of population-based studies indicates that autistic individuals face an estimated eight-fold greater risk of death by suicide compared to non-autistic peers.
  • Meta-analyses estimate that approximately one in three autistic individuals experience suicidal ideation, and up to 25% attempt suicide.

The Diagnostic Shadow: Misidentification in Clinical Practice

In clinical practice, I have worked with many adults who were only identified as autistic in their forties or fifties. They had cycled through decades of psychotherapy, psychiatric admissions, and addiction treatment before anyone asked the questions that helped them understand why they experienced the world so intensely.

I have encountered countless individuals diagnosed with major depressive disorder, conduct disorder, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, or borderline personality disorder whose clinical presentations were better explained by underlying autism.

For many undiagnosed autistic people, their psychiatric symptoms reflect a lifelong struggle to navigate a neurodivergent mind without sufficient insight and support.

Furthermore, autistic individuals without intellectual impairment or extreme functional impairment, often referred to as "level one", "high functioning", or "mildly autistic") are substantially more likely than the general population to develop substance use disorders. Alcohol and illicit substances frequently serve as chemical masking tools and coping mechanisms to dull sensory overload and social anxiety. When these substances wear off, the underlying sensory overload and social exhaustion return, compounded by the physiological toll of withdrawal. This cycle fuels autistic burnout, a state of profound physical, mental, and emotional exhaustion that is often misdiagnosed as treatment-resistant depression. Despite this, screening for autism is rarely included in standard protocols for crisis support or substance use disorders.

The Limitations of Standardized Protocols

When individuals seek mental health support, clinicians are trained to follow standardized assessment and treatment protocols. However, these methods can inadvertently exacerbate an undiagnosed autistic person’s distress. Evaluation interviews and group therapy in highly stimulating environments, cognitive behavioral strategies that demand increased self-monitoring, and intense focus on self-care strategies can compound the very social anxiety and cognitive exhaustion the patient is trying to escape. We end up treating downstream symptoms while overlooking the upstream neurodivergent vulnerability.

We must listen better, but we also need to question better.

While evidence-based practices are essential, clinical protocols must evolve to integrate new evidence on neurodivergence. In addition to standard lethality assessments, clinicians can dig deeper with more nuanced questions to explore hidden risk factors:

  • “What are you seeking relief from?”
  • “Does the world frequently feel too loud, bright, or physically overwhelming to you?”
  • “Does it feel as though the world was not built for the way your mind works?”
  • "Who in your life really understands you?"
  • “How can we help you feel more comfortable in the world?"

Shifting the Clinical Paradigm

National suicide prevention strategies rightly focus on high-risk populations, including veterans, LGBTQIA+ communities, and indigenous peoples. However, autism is too often categorized as a co-occurring developmental condition rather than recognized as an independent and robust risk factor for suicide. That distinction matters. If we do not routinely screen for autism in adults presenting with addiction, self-harm, treatment-resistant mental illness, or suicidality, we miss critical opportunities for life-saving intervention.

Integrating a neurodivergent-affirming lens shifts the clinical question away from, "Why is this person failing to cope?" to, "What has this person been coping with, unsupported, for their entire life?" This paradigm shift can transform care. It prompts clinicians to address sensory accommodation, mitigate chronic burnout, and help people develop safe, neurodivergent-affirming coping strategies.

If we are serious about preventing suicide and overdose deaths, autism screening must be integrated into routine psychiatric and addiction assessments. Our mental health workforce needs targeted training to recognize adult autistic presentations, and clinical research must treat autism as a primary risk factor. By looking beyond diagnoses to understand nuanced individual experiences and risk factors, we can identify new pathways to intervention. The answer begins with asking better questions, not only about how someone died, but about how they lived.

item.title: Get to the Root of Conflict with Radical Repair
item.description:
Relationships

Get to the Root of Conflict with Radical Repair

Resolving issues at their root lays the groundwork for resilience and trust.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Disagreements don't mean your relationship is in trouble.
  • Relational resilience can help us, and our relationship, bounce back after conflict.
  • Address the root of the conflict rather than the disagreement itself.

In an episode of his podcast, Travis Kelce stated that he and his wife Taylor Swift have never had a fight. George Clooney has made the same claim about him and his wife, Amal. Is this a level of perfect coupledom that we should all be striving for? And if we do happen to argue with our partner, does that mean our relationship is doomed?

The answer is no. There may be couples who never fight, friends who always get along, and families that live in perfect harmony, but they are the exception, not the rule. Conflict is a natural byproduct of interacting with other humans. If handled well, it can make our connections even stronger.

Why conflict is normal

Conflict is inevitable in human relationships. Whenever two people bring their own needs, histories, and perspectives to a shared space, some friction is bound to occur. Even if both people are heavily invested in the relationship and they already have a strong, loving connection, disagreements and arguments will happen. Research backs this up. In a 2012 study, 60 couples with high relationship satisfaction (averaging over 6 on a 7-point scale) reported an average of 2.32 negative incidents or conflicts over a week. Some reported as many as nine (Schumann, 2012). Even “happy” couples argue regularly.

Arguing isn’t a sign of failure or a red flag for the relationship. What matters is how it’s handled. A recent study found that conflict only predicts lower relationship satisfaction when relational resilience—the ability to recover and reconnect after conflict—is low (Kaygas and Özbay, 2023). When relational resilience is high, it acts as a buffer; if we do happen to argue, it doesn’t negatively affect our relationship.

Relational resilience is not something you either have or don’t. It develops through experience. Every time we resolve conflict effectively, we get better at it. And when we know that we can withstand the occasional disagreement or argument in our relationship, the connection gets stronger. Over time, this creates a sense of security, knowing that the relationship is resilient.

The solid fix: Radical repair

This is where radical repair comes in. The word “radical” comes from the Latin radix, which means “root.” Think of the roots in plants. Without deep, healthy roots, the plant can’t absorb nutrients from the soil. And without this nourishment, the roots grow shallow, leaving the plant fragile and unstable. Relationships work the same way.

Radical repair means getting to the root of the conflict.
Source: Scott Annandale / Used with permission

A quick, dismissive “sorry” after an argument is like sprinkling a few drops of water on the topsoil. It may temporarily smooth things over, but it doesn’t address what caused the rupture, the root of the issue. Over time, unresolved issues accumulate beneath the surface.

Radical repair means going deeper. Instead of focusing only on the surface conflict—like arriving late for a lunch date or forgetting to do a chore—it means exploring the root of the conflict. For example, a disagreement about household chores may not be about dishes at all. It might reflect a bigger concern about fairness, respect, or unpaid labor. A friend’s anger at your lateness might be more about feeling disrespected than about the actual time they spent waiting for you at the restaurant. When only the surface issue is addressed, the same arguments tend to recur. Understanding the root cause of the conflict can interrupt this pattern.

The benefits of repair

There is ample psychological evidence that radical repair, and not avoiding conflict, is what sustains relationships. And it’s not only important for romantic partners. Research on families shows that children benefit when their parents repair conflicts effectively, particularly through sincere, effective apologies. These children tend to have better mental health than those whose parents don’t apologize (Lee and colleagues, 2023).

What’s needed for repair depends on many factors, including the harm caused and the people involved. Gender, culture, and situational factors may all play a role. But here are some general strategies for radical repair when conflict happens:

  • Take responsibility for your actions. Don’t make excuses.
  • Don’t assume you know how the other person feels. Ask them.
  • Show genuine concern for their feelings.
  • Work together to find ways to avoid similar conflicts in the future.

It’s important to remember that radical repair is a two-way street. Although one person needs to take accountability, the other needs to remain open to understanding and rebuilding.

Does this mean you should pick fights with people for a stronger relationship? No, of course not. But don’t be afraid of conflict either.

If there is a problem that you haven’t addressed, don’t let it simmer. Tend to the roots rather than the surface. Lean into radical repair to transform the friction into the foundation for a stronger, more resilient connection.

In this blog, I’ll address other ways you can use radical repair to strengthen your relationships, rebuild trust, and reconcile after mistakes. Whether you are repairing a relationship with another person, forgiving yourself, or navigating a fractured community, radical repair can help you recover grace, connection, and meaning in an imperfect world.

item.title: More Principles of Sexual Health
item.description:
Sex

More Principles of Sexual Health

Key questions to ask yourself and every partner about your current sex life.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Mutual pleasure means prioritizing curiosity and authentic enjoyment for all partners.
  • Ignoring pleasure in sex education deprives children and adults of vital sexual health knowledge.
  • Sexual exploitation includes manipulation, not just force—true consent requires open communication.
Source: Shvetsa/Pexels

This post is part 2 in a series. Read part 1 here.

Pleasure: Mutual Pleasure Matters

Pleasure goes beyond simply having orgasms. It’s about curiosity, connection, and caring about your partner’s experience. Pleasure will look different for different people’s or a couple’s experiences, and it can change across the lifespan. People in ethical non-monogamous or polyamorous relationships will also need to consciously explore how their stimulation and experiences with one partner may differ greatly from their sex life with another partner.

Caregivers or parents will often ignore the topic of pleasure when providing sex education for their children at each stage of their developmental growth. Many adults are uncomfortable and lack their own education to provide thoughtful and loving guidance to their children or young ones about the importance of experiencing pleasure by themselves or with a partner, and of being equally committed to offering to give pleasure to their partners. Most parents were not taught this and, because of their own embarrassment or shame, are quick to defend this decision by stating that their kids are too young for sex and/or masturbation.

This same blind spot or denial around discussing sexual pleasure can also occur when adult children are caring for their elderly parents who are involved in sexual relationships. Adult children, while fully grown adults, are still their parents’ children and have the “ick” factor to get over in thinking about and frankly discussing sexuality with their parents and, in some cases, with the retirement or nursing home staff where they live.

Pleasure is about balancing all the other sexual health principles with each partner’s authentic sexual curiosity. When a partner “fakes an orgasm” or pretends they are enjoying stimulation a partner is providing, they are contributing to their partner’s beliefs that what they are doing is actually what the receiver is enjoying. The sexual encounter is then not mutual or authentic at all.

Source: KetutSubiyanto/Pexels

Non-Exploitation: Sex Should Never Involve Manipulation or Coercion

Sexual exploitation happens when someone uses their power or dishonesty in a sexual relationship. This power imbalance may arise from differences in partners’ cognitive ability, intoxication level, or other circumstances that limit one person’s capacity to give full consent. Exploitation can also come in the form of verbal or non-verbal manipulation, psychological pressure, and/or guilt-inducing communication by one partner to another.

Explicit force doesn’t need to be involved for exploitative sex to occur. For example, when one partner repeatedly threatens to end a relationship unless the other partner agrees to sexual activity, they are psychologically pressuring their partner and undermining joint sexual decision-making.

Another example of exploitation occurs when one partner has sex outside the agreement they’ve made with their partner (whether they have promised sexual exclusivity or are in an ethical non-monogamous relationship). When the betraying partner doesn’t use any STI protection with the secondary or outside partners without telling their primary partner and proceeds to continue having unprotected sex with their primary partner, this is exploitative sex.

What the betraying partner has exploited is their primary partner’s trust and lack of knowledge so that they aren’t able to fully consent to having unprotected sex. They have thus put their partner’s sexual health at risk while also breaking their promise of their sexual monogamy agreement. This is also true for partners in an ENM or poly agreement, for example when the primary couple agreed they would always have protected penetrative sex in consensual non-monogamous experiences with other partners.

Source: Cottonbro/Pexels

Prevention: Precautions for Physical Health

This is perhaps what people think of when the topic of sexual health comes up. It’s clearly imperative to discuss safer sex practices like condoms and other forms of birth control to prevent STIs as well as unwanted pregnancy. For example, before becoming sexually active with a new partner, each partner may decide to get tested for STIs and openly show and discuss the results so they can make informed decisions together.

In addition, the sexual health principle of prevention also includes issues like partners agreeing not to continue penetration (anal or vaginal) if the receiving partner is having pain. As Certified Sex Therapists, taking painful penetration off the table for a little while until the condition can be treated medically is one of the first interventions proposed to partners when one partner reports pain during intercourse or anal sex. Psycho-education is provided in sex therapy on the long-term physical and emotional damage that follows when people continually grind through a painful sexual experience.

The consequences of pushing oneself or one’s partner through a painful penetration can include trauma symptoms to future initiations of intimacy. Post-trauma symptoms like freeze, flight, fight, and fawning are common blocks to people having painful sex. The principle of prevention is all about making informed decisions as an individual for one’s sex and one’s partner and/or as a couple when it comes to partnered sex.

The Six Sexual Health Principles Mindset

Contrary to many people’s beliefs, sexual health isn’t only measured by frequency, fantasy, or comparisons to what the rest of the country is doing. It’s built on mutual consent, pleasure, honesty, shared values, respect, and protection of oneself and of whoever one has a sexual experience with. These six sexual health principles help all types of partners and/or couples build a healthy and meaningful sexual relationship. Instead of asking, “Are we having enough sex?” try asking yourself and your partner(s):

  • Do we feel safe communicating about sex?
  • Do we adhere to each other’s boundaries?
  • Are we honest about our needs?
  • Do we both feel respected?
  • Are we in full agreement as to how we will protect one another’s health?

Furthermore, these sexual health principles are never static. A healthy sexual relationship requires ongoing conversations with partners because all people’s bodies, desires, health, and circumstances will change over time, including from day to day and hour by hour.

item.title: You Need This Trait More Than Chemistry in Your Relationship
item.description:
Self-Control

You Need This Trait More Than Chemistry in Your Relationship

Chemistry defines the beginning, but this trait predicts longevity.

Posted August 5, 2026

Source: Timur Weber / Pexels

Attraction in a relationship is a measure of intensity. That is, how strongly two people are drawn to each other, how quickly the connection forms, and how much energy the relationship generates in its early months. What it does not measure is durability, because durability isn’t tested by attraction. It’s tested by conflict, disappointment, and the accumulated friction of two people living inside each other’s lives for years at a time.

A relationship can score extremely high on chemistry and still fail the only test that determines its longevity; that test happens later, under different conditions, and chemistry was never built to pass it.

The quality that predicts longevity has been hiding in plain sight for over 2000 years, under a name most people associate with philosophy rather than psychology: Temperance. Classical thinkers used it to describe the capacity to feel a powerful impulse and choose not to act on it.

Contemporary psychology inherited the same concept and gave it a clinical label, self-regulation, but kept its place among the small set of traits considered foundational to human character.

Where the Trait Actually Operates

Temperance does its work in a specific, recurring moment: immediately after a partner has done something careless, dismissive, or unfair, and before the other partner has responded. In that narrow window, an impulse toward retaliation is nearly automatic. It’s easy to snap back with a sharp reply, a withdrawal or even a punishing silence. What happens next depends almost entirely on whether that impulse gets acted on or interrupted.

Relationship researchers refer to the interruption itself as accommodation: the act of inhibiting a destructive response to a partner’s provocation and substituting a constructive one instead. A 2001 study published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology found that dispositional self-control was one of the strongest and most consistent predictors identified — people higher in self-control were reliably better at performing this exact substitution, swapping the retaliatory reflex for a response that served the relationship rather than the ego. The finding held across multiple independent studies, which is notable in a field where most single effects don't replicate that cleanly.

A 2020 study published in Aggressive Behavior that tracked heavy-drinking couples over 30 days in their daily lives found a related, if more modest, pattern outside the lab: depleted self-control was linked to more anger and arguing with a partner in the hours that followed; however, the authors note the effect was modest, and the relationship ran both ways, with arguing also draining self-control in turn.

Why This Trait Outweighs Attraction Over Time

The reason this trait outperforms chemistry as a long-term predictor is arithmetic rather than romantic. A relationship generates thousands of these small provocation-and-response cycles over the course of a decade.

Individually, almost none of them are serious enough to end a relationship. Collectively, they are the relationship, in the sense that they are what most of a long partnership is actually made of. A couple’s trajectory is set less by how often these moments occur and more by which impulse wins each time. Chemistry does not influence that outcome; by the time the provoking moment arrives, whatever chemistry contributed has already been spent.

article continues after advertisement

The relationship between self-control and good partnership is not perfectly linear, and the research is careful about this. Some of the same investigators who established the link between self-control and accommodation published a 2013 study in Psychological Science finding that people lower in self-control are, in certain circumstances, more willing to make immediate personal sacrifices for a partner; their prosocial impulse fires before self-interest has time to intervene. Self-control is not a universal advantage; it is specifically valuable at the moment of provocation, not a trait that should be maximized without limit.

There is a related failure mode worth naming directly: restraint that has curdled into suppression. A partner who never appears frustrated is not necessarily practicing temperance. In some cases, that pattern reflects a partner who has stopped registering their own needs at all, which produces the appearance of equanimity without any of its substance. The clinically meaningful version of this trait is not the absence of a reaction. It is the presence of a brief interval between the reaction and the response, long enough for the better instinct to overtake the faster one.

Can This Trait Be Built?

Unlike attraction, which either exists between two people or doesn’t, this trait has a documented mechanism for strengthening it, and it isn’t willpower. Researchers studying emotion regulation have found that people can widen that crucial interval between provocation and response by changing their vantage point on the moment itself, by stepping back to observe the exchange as an outside witness would, rather than experiencing it entirely from the inside. This is known as self-distancing, and a 2017 review published in Advances in Experimental Social Psychology, surveying over a decade of research on it, describes it being tested directly in moments of provocation and romantic conflict, consistently finding less aggressive thinking and fewer aggressive responses in the heat of an argument, and more constructive behavior toward a partner during an actual disagreement, among people who adopt this outside perspective rather than staying immersed in the moment.

The mechanism is not complicated, even if it takes practice to use in real time. It amounts to a shift in vantage point rather than a suppression of feeling. That small reframe of perspective appears to be what creates the interval in the first place.

The trait that predicts whether two people stay together in 20 years operates in a moment attraction doesn’t reach. And unlike attraction, it’s a moment a person has some actual say over.

A version of this post also appears on Forbes.com.

item.title: Probability as a Number, Probability as a Personality Test
item.description:
Personality

Probability as a Number, Probability as a Personality Test

Why statistics can freeze you or free you.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Probability statistics looks at the likelihood of future events based on past events.
  • In some cases, people look at probability to justify inaction.
  • The same statistics, however, can be viewed as an incentive to take action.
  • People with binary cognitive frameworks can use probability statistics to justify taking risk.

Probability is the branch of mathematics that measures the likelihood of an event occurring. In this entry, we examine how you can use probability statistics to free or freeze yourself.

Probability Is a Number

One way of looking at probability is as an unemotional predictive index. You look down at your mobile device in the morning and read about the probability of snow during the day. That number governs your shoe selection and perhaps the route you will take to work. Your reaction to that number reveals your level of risk-taking when faced with uncertainty. In that sense, your reaction to that number becomes a demonstration of your personality.

Probability Is a Projective Test

According to the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics, data collected in 2025 show that the probability of a new business failing within five years is 49.4 percent. That is the statistic. Does that number frighten you or excite you?

Sanjay Manandhar is an MIT-educated engineer, an entrepreneur, and an author. His 2026 book The Why Not Advantage is an exploration of probability statistics as a projective test about yourself. He writes, “Low probability odds may be statistically valid for a population or large sample. But do those odds apply to you? I wrote this book to give you the same permission I gave myself: The permission to ask, ‘Why not?’”

Probability is not an external truth. It is a number that tells you what has happened to others in the past. When you use that number to justify inaction, you reveal yourself. If you have an entrepreneurial framework, however, you can interpret the same number differently. As Mr. Manandhar states, “When the world told me ‘unlikely,’ I heard ‘possible.’”

Helen Greiner’s Career

Mr. Manandhar describes the career of his fellow MIT classmate Helen Greiner. When Ms. Greiner graduated from MIT in 1989, only 10 percent of her graduating class were female. The vast majority of 1989 MIT graduates wanted to begin careers with well-known companies that offered good salaries, excellent training, and immediate professional respect.

Helen Greiner, on the other hand, decided to take an “improbable” route. She began her career by turning science fiction into reality: Making robots. She and two colleagues founded IRobot. She was its President for 18 years. Since 2020, Ms. Greiner has been CEO and Chair of the robot-gardening company Tertill.

Probability as Permission

Probability statistics for an entrepreneur can indeed be interpreted as “possible.” For others, probability can be interpreted as “permission.” Binary thinking refers to a tendency to view things as black/white, 0/1, good/bad, and more. According to Sabrina Zohar, nearly all of us engage in binary thinking during the year. The tendency towards binary thinking increases with stress and sleep deprivation (2025).

article continues after advertisement

For example, “I’m scheduled to be a passenger on a commercial airline going from New York City to Los Angeles. My plane could crash. I could die.”

The above statement is factually correct. Framing the issue in a binary way (could versus could not) makes fear a natural consequence.

The same issue, however, can be reframed as a probability question. Use an Artificial Intelligence tool to ask, “What is the probability of a commercial airline crashing on the New York City to Los Angeles route?” Below is Gemini’s response: “0.000001 percent, making it one of the safest heavily traveled corridors in the world.”

Summary and Conclusions:

Probability statistics are numbers based on large samples of past events. The numbers are neutral. It is the interaction between these numbers and your cognitive framework that makes the difference. When looking at probability statistics, ask yourself if you are viewing the numbers as permission to act or justification to avoid action.

item.title: The Cost of Losing Self-Respect in Addiction
item.description:
Addiction

The Cost of Losing Self-Respect in Addiction

We tend to shrink ourselves and our world when we lack self-respect.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Active in our addictions, we shrink ourselves so that we and our use may go unnoticed.
  • We may believe that we do not deserve to take up space in the world, which is a deficit of self-respect.
  • Self-respect is an achievement of moral development that depends on love, care, and support.
  • Addictions can cause us to lose self-respect. Does a deficit of self-respect contribute to addiction?

Active in our addictions, our worlds often shrink. We prune people from our lives who question our use. We remove ourselves from events and activities that once brought us joy. We become less willing to do or try new things. Where before possibilities had seemed like opportunities, now they just feel daunting and even threatening.

We make ourselves smaller. We start to take up less space in our own lives. As someone once said, I felt like a mouse running around the trim board of my own life. Our making ourselves smaller goes hand in hand with our social and physical worlds contracting; they aid and abet each other.

Why do we skitter around the margins of our own lives?

Some of us want to go unnoticed. We may tell ourselves, better to stay off the radar screen than have people judging us. We may take our not being noticed as evidence that we aren’t doing so badly.

If people do notice us and our use, we may automatically assume that they are judging us in the same harsh ways that we judge ourselves. Of course, there are plenty of instances when this is true. We cannot even imagine that they are standing by us and offering their support because, well, we don’t deserve it.

Others of us believe that we do not deserve to take up space in anyone’s life, including our own. This is especially true for people who lack self-respect.

Self-respect

Self-respect is an achievement within moral development; it is a lived conviction that a person has intrinsic worth and dignity. It is a basic sense that “I matter.” Self-respect is created against a background of care, love, and security. A person develops self-respect through having the opportunities to engage with others. Self-respect is not innate.

A person with self-respect understands that she deserves to be treated respectfully by others because she has the same moral worth as everyone else. She also understands that she needs to treat herself in ways that recognize and preserve her dignity and autonomy.

Self-respect is what enables a person to judge that she is measuring up not just to others but to her own standards. When a person with self-respect recognizes that she is not meeting her own measure, she may change her actions so that she preserves her self-respect.

Self-respect and addiction

Self-respect is easily lost in addiction. There are many cases where a person has had self-respect but has lost it, often through their own actions. Someone who has had a good, meaningful, and happy life may lose respect for himself when he develops an addiction later in life and begins to act in ways that are out of character.

We may start trading away our values and commitments. We may do things that cut against our grain. Instead of seeing ourselves as having dignity and worth, we come to see ourselves as insignificant and worthless. We start to treat ourselves this way.

The more we feel worthless, the more we contract into ourselves. In the worst throes of addiction, the world is reduced to us and our substances and behaviors. Our minds and the entire world may seem like a hellscape.

Some people have only ever had a very small degree of self-respect because they never had the opportunity to develop the skills and arts that underpin self-respect. Where love, care, and security are missing, it becomes far more difficult for a child to develop the arts and skills that are necessary to create, reinforce, and cherish self-respect.

Children who have been traumatized may have had many of the opportunities necessary to develop self-respect foreclosed. A child who has never been treated with love and respect or treated in ways that twine abuse with love will not have the opportunities to learn how to create, act on, and protect their self-respect. They have not been treated respectfully by others, so it is challenging to learn how to treat themselves and have a clear sense of what they rightly deserve.

Traumatized children, and later adolescents and adults, are more likely to develop an addiction than children who have not been traumatized.

While a loss of self-respect is a consequence of addiction, I believe a lack of self-respect is also a driving force of addiction. People who have experienced childhood trauma and haven’t been able to practice self-respect have already known a world of pain, insecurity, and uncertainty. They may already have a sense of just how unfair the world is along with a fatalism about their place in it. They understand what it is like to have few good opportunities available to them. They see others around them suffering and can’t even imagine their lives going differently.

When a person believes she has no value and that people like her deserve no better, the allure of addictive substances and behaviors may seem great. She may know that her world is full of pain and suffering; shrinking that world and finding some relief from the suffering makes sense.

Those addictive substances and behaviors can also ignite a sense of being alive, having fun, and making connections to others, all of which childhood trauma hinders. The addictive substances and behaviors most often bring us something we want or need in the beginning. Their bill comes due at some point, putting whatever shards of self-respect a person has at risk.

In recovery, we begin to gain or regain self-respect, which is crucial to flourishing.

item.title: You're Not Bailing Out Your Adult Child, You're Buying Proof
item.description:
Parenting

You're Not Bailing Out Your Adult Child, You're Buying Proof

A one-word writing exercise exposes what your bailouts are really about.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • Somewhere between 'just this once' and now, that became the policy.
  • Your kid isn't testing your love. They're testing a rule nobody ever wrote down.
  • Are you providing money to truly help (and is it really helping)? Or is it hush money for your own guilt?

Carol looked up at me on our virtual call and said, "Hold on, you want me to do what?" I gently further encouraged her by repeating my prompt. She then wrote each number in the left column first. That's right, I'm talking about every transfer, loan, and rescue to her son over the past year, totaled up on a legal pad. But what actually gave her pause wasn't the list of numbers or the total dollars, for that matter. Rather, it was the second column I'd asked her to add to the right: one word (specifically, the feelings) next to each entry, for what she felt in each moment she said yes.

"Relief," she wrote next to the first one. "Dread" next to the third. Then, beside the largest number on the page—the security deposit that got her son out of a bad living situation fast—she wrote a word that surprised her more than the dollar amount ever could: "Proof." I asked, "Proof of what?" Carol's jaw dropped, and she replied, "I guess that 'first responder' uniform you told me I have been wearing is coming out of my sense of guilt and my incessant need to prove that I care."

That Precious Proof: "That we're good parents, that we didn't turn our backs"

I've watched this happen more times than I can count when parents truly open up to me. Parents assume the hard money conversation with their adult kids is about money. It rarely is. Once cash starts moving between a parent and a grown child, it ceases to be just cash. It becomes a way of saying things the family never says out loud: love, but also fear, control, guilt, and forgiveness. A $600 car repair can carry all of that at once, which is why it feels so much bigger than $400.

What surprises parents isn't that pattern. It's what's underneath it: their family already has a policy for how money moves. Nobody wrote it down. It got built anyway, one anxious yes at a time. Parents tell me almost the same line once they see it on paper: "I don't know when yes turned into our entire plan."

The Fear of Changing the Rules of the Bank of Mom and Dad

Since when does the bank of mom and dad never get to change its terms? That's the argument at the center of my new book, The Bank of Mom and Dad Has New Rules. For so many parents, it gets to the point where it feels very complicated, more complicated than it actually needs to be, for them to realize that "The Bank" just needs new terms. By the way, this usually does not mean a locked door. My point here is that closing "the bank" outright often isn't the answer, yet running it on autopilot isn't either. The answer is going back and choosing the terms on purpose, together, out loud, instead of discovering them by accident every time the phone pings with a new text message request or even if the phone actually rings.

In healthy families, thoughtful decisions about providing financial help come down to a handful of decisions nobody wants to make in the middle of a crisis. Gift or loan, decided by whom, and when? What happens if a payment gets missed once? Is there one honest emergency exception, named ahead of time, so the whole thing doesn't fall apart the first time real life gets messy? Is a spontaneous gift okay? But how can it stay a gift and not a precedent for future yeses?

The Takeaway

None of that is about learning to say no. It's about not improvising a yes or a no from scratch, under pressure, with your kid on the line. And it's not only parents who want this. Adult children have told me, more than once, that they wanted this conversation before their parents did—they just didn't know how to raise it without sounding like they were asking for less love, not more clarity.

item.title: Life Before and After Treatment for Schizophrenia
item.description:
Psychosis

Life Before and After Treatment for Schizophrenia

Personal Perspective: How schizophrenia shaped two versions of my life.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • A person living in treatment for schizophrenia can have a different life than one who is untreated.
  • I had been an honors student at USC before untreated schizophrenia led me to drop out and become homeless.
  • There is hope today for people with schizophrenia thanks to the newer medications and clozapine.
  • Antipsychotic medication can restore even a severely ill person to a point of recovery and productivity.
Source: Selenee51 / PIxabay

Some days when I get out of bed and begin getting ready for my day, I look in the mirror and am amazed. How can I really the same person I used to be when I was homeless and deeply affected by untreated schizophrenia?

Growing up, I was the honor student, the violinist, the daughter, the sister, and the friend. I loved my family. Life was full of friends at church, in school, and at the Cleveland Institute of Music where I studied violin.

I never imagined that the next phase of my life, right as I was turning 21 and becoming an adult, would involve losing everything I loved and becoming homeless.

As I student attending USC, one of my favorite classes was differential equations. As schizophrenia symptoms began to insidiously emerge, my mind became distracted. This is probably why I scored a B and not an A. But I still greatly enjoyed the class and considered switching my major from biochemistry to engineering.

I keenly remember years later while very ill, going back to the classroom where I had studied differential equations. That afternoon, I sat in the empty classroom, alone, eating whatever garbage I could find. I was always surprised by just how much food the students had left. I could not grasp the magnitude of how far I had fallen in so short a time.

I remember practicing violin for four hours a day in high school. When I graduated from high school and began classes at USC, I quickly won the position of concertmaster of their community orchestra. I remember coming onto the stage as everyone clapped for me and tuning the orchestra. My friends who were other freshmen from my dorm watched in the audience, surprised by my musical ability.

Years later, I would go back to that same building where I had once performed, but this time it was not to play the violin. Near the auditorium, there were two full private bathrooms that could be locked, some of the only ones like that on the campus. I would put my feet, one at a time, into the sink and wash myself as quickly as I could in privacy. I even remember washing my long hair in the sink. Because I washed it with hand soap, when it dried, it was oily. I was so out of touch that I did not even mind wandering around the campus afterwards with soaking wet hair.

When I began USC, I was very active in a community church. When I was later homeless, I would often go to the place where the church had once been located (as it later moved) and stare into space as I waited for people to leave, hoping I could find some good trashed food to eat.

I cannot fully comprehend my history living as two different versions of myself which are such polar opposites.

When I think of the two different versions of myself I have experienced because of illness, I stand amazed at the power of antipsychotic medication. How can it be that single oral pills can radically transform a person from a lonely homeless stranger into a thriving, productive member of society? The difference between untreated and treated schizophrenia can be vastly different when the right medication is found for each individual. Compliance in treatment is also vital.

I am grateful everyday for my sustained recovery. I cannot even imagine living this life prior to the discovery of antipsychotic medication in the 1950s. I would have been institutionalized for life, living everyday with voices in my mind and hallucinations.

One of the biggest barriers to treatment for schizophrenia is lack of insight, as people cannot tell how much they have changed and how ill they are. I understand this so well. When I went to the room where the math class had been and the bathroom right by the auditorium, I thought I had not changed. I thought I could take advanced biochemistry again and score another A. But that would have been impossible at that time.

Regaining healthy Insight often is accompanied by grief and feelings of profound loss, as you have to make peace with having been so exceedingly ill and out of touch with reality. But if my schizophrenia had remained untreated, I most likely would have faced a future of severe illness, the inability to preform purposeful work, and a life lived in the shadows of society.

Today, on medication, there is hope for the sickest street people in our society. I know this because I was one of them.

item.title: The Strengths Gap Fueling AI Burnout at Work
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Strengths Gap Fueling AI Burnout at Work

Why losing sight of what you're good at might be driving you toward burnout.

Posted August 5, 2026

Key points
  • People regularly using AI at work experience a drop in strengths use and a higher risk of burnout.
  • AI disrupts flow when you're a passive rather than active user of it.
  • How to create a simple AI Strengths Map to help you actively collaborate with AI.

Is using AI making your work faster, and your days a little emptier, at the same time? Is it limiting your creative outlets? Taking away chances to solve problems with a teammate? Leaving you feeling, if you're honest, just a little dumber?

We surveyed more than 800 Australian workers, and those regularly using AI at work doubted themselves far more than those who used it rarely (53 percent versus 37 percent), used their strengths less (38 percent versus 60 percent), and were more likely to feel burned out (49 percent versus 32 percent). Confidence and well-being drop when we have fewer opportunities to do what we do best at work—use our strengths.

This is because when you’re able to use your strengths to tackle tasks at work, you experience the state of flow. You become deeply engaged in the work you’re doing, proud of what you’re accomplishing, and are left energized and satisfied. It’s the feeling you get of being “in the zone” or “one with the music,” and it is where your best work happens.

Using AI tends to disrupt your flow state. Studies have found AI tools shift you from active creation to more passive supervision as you write (and rewrite) prompts, digest the reasoning, and evaluate and edit the output. When we outsource our thinking and creativity to an AI tool, it can induce complacency, lead to overreliance, and cause us to undervalue our own capabilities.

The shift from creating to evaluating costs you more than focus. A 2026 study of professionals found that passive AI use, just copying what it produces, drops your confidence, your sense of ownership over the work, and how meaningful it feels.

However, researchers have also found that when you use your strengths wisely and actively collaborate with AI tools, you can sustain your state of flow. For example, if you create the first draft and then work with AI to help you refine and edit, you stay just as engaged in the work as if you'd done it alone. Or if you use AI to get the repetitive, draining parts of a task off your plate, it can free you to stay absorbed in the parts that stretch you and help you grow.

How can you map your strengths to the ways you’re working with AI?

Build Your AI Strengths Map

You can create an AI Strengths Map by following these steps:

  1. Create your map: Grab a sheet of paper and divide it into three columns.
  2. List your regular tasks: In the middle column, list the tasks that make up most of your week. Next to each one, name the skill that makes the real difference: speed, creativity, judgment, collaboration, and so on. Think of this as a dynamic list so you can keep adding to it as needed.
  3. List your strengths: In the left-hand column, write down your top strengths. These are the things you’re good at and enjoy doing at work. You can spot them by thinking about the times you’ve felt engaged, energized, and most effective at work. Which strengths were you using? You can also use the free 10-minute VIA Survey or ask people who know your work well.
  4. List the strengths of AI: In the right column, write down the top strengths of AI. What does it do well when it comes to the tasks you need to tackle? Where does it add value to your work? Where does it free you from repetitive or draining tasks?
  5. Align strengths with tasks: Draw lines to connect your strengths to the tasks either because you're the best person for the job, or because it's a capability worth protecting for later. Then do the same from AI's column. Ask which tasks suit what it does well: the ones that drain you, the ones where speed or consistency beats you, or the ones where your active collaboration will deliver better results.

As your week unfolds, use your AI Strengths Map to guide you on the most enjoyable and effective ways to get your work done. This can also be a great exercise for teams to do together. Ask everyone to bring their map to a meeting, and you'll quickly spot how to draw better on each other’s strengths and where the AI tools work best.

How are you using your strengths to work wisely and well with AI?
